conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been feeling nauseous and vomiting since this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right after I took my pills on an empty stomach. I couldn’t keep anything down all day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You went to the ER earlier and got fluids, Zofran, and Dilaudid. But the nausea didn’t improve much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. I still felt sick. The Zofran ODT didn’t help at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any belly pain, diarrhea, or constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No stomach pain. Just my usual back pain. But I’ve been nauseous all day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Your labs came back — no infection, no kidney issues, and your glucose was 87 when you arrived. That’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not DKA or anything serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not this time. Your anion gap is normal, so we’re not worried about ketoacidosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why does this keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, it’s likely related to your gastroparesis — delayed stomach emptying from diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my stomach just doesn’t move food along?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And taking meds on an empty stomach can trigger nausea. We’ll keep you on bowel rest tonight — no food, just IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Will I be able to eat tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips in the morning. If you tolerate that, we’ll try light food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I’m worried about my sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your fingersticks. Since you’re not eating, we lowered your Lantus to 24 units tonight to avoid low sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually take 28 at night. Is it safe to go lower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, temporarily. Once you’re eating normally again, you’ll go back to 28.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still getting your amoxicillin, levofloxacin, and pantoprazole for your H. pylori treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Reglan? That usually helps with nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding the oral Reglan for now since you can’t keep pills down. But we’ll restart it when you can eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about pain? My back’s been bothering me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can have tramadol as needed. We’ll avoid morphine — you’re allergic, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and Prochlorperazine too. Tramadol is fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I haven’t vomited since last night. Can I try some water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with ice chips and clear liquids. If that stays down, we’ll advance to a light meal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And my blood sugar was low this morning — 46.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that was during the night. It confirms we did the right thing lowering your Lantus. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I should keep it at 24 until I’m eating normally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Once you’re back on regular meals, go back to 28 units at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with the clear liquids. Ready to try a soft meal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m hungry. Maybe some toast and applesauce?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll bring that shortly. And we’re restarting Reglan with meals to help with stomach emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been doing really well — tolerating food, no nausea, no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Can I go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you. Just a few things to go over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, what do I need to know?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your meds, including the antibiotics for H. pylori. Take Reglan with meals, not four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep Lantus at 24 units tonight. When your appetite is back to normal, increase it to 28.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Any follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, see your primary doctor in a few weeks. Call if nausea returns or you can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel a low sugar coming on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Treat it with fast-acting sugar — juice or glucose tabs. And check your levels four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have my meter with me. I’ll keep up with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You’re cleared to go home. Take it easy, eat small meals, and don’t take pills on an empty stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — my back pain is better, but should I restart my tramadol at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as needed. Just don’t exceed one every four hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Zofran — same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one every six hours as needed for nausea. But call if you need it more than twice in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll play it safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.
